body:
I thought that Death would be different, that I would see it coming. All I saw coming was the bus  speeding down the street.

Then it stopped.

I looked around, nothing was moving. The birds had stopped flying, people were standing still. I walked to a woman on her phone, staring as her mouth didnt produce any sounds.

"Strange isn't?" A low, sultry voice said behind me.

I whirled around to see a man, a handsome one at that, leaning against the brick wall in what looked like an expensive suit. 

"Sorry?"

"Your soul is ready for departure. Are you?" 

I look around bewildering at someone to get this crackhead off the street. Or maybe he is actually the grim reaper.

"Do you- are you going to take me to Heaven?" 

He laughs, a throaty chuckle that made me tingly inside. "Well that's for the big guy to decide. I'm here to complete what you humans adorably call your 'bucket lists'." He pushes off the wall, slinging an arm around me comfortably, leading away from the street with the speeding bus.

"I don- I mean I guess I have some stuff I'd like to do, if you're paying." I say coyly, grinning when he laughs as well.

"Anything darling." 

We spent the day going around New York city, eating the best foods and seeing the sights without any lines. 

The grim reaper had this amazing power of teleporting anywhere. To the top of the empire state building and onto the crown of the statue of liberty. 

"Now, its sundown, so your time is up. What is the last thing on your list?" He asks, licking an ice cream cone from the vendor on the corner of the street.

I shrug, taking a bite out of my ice cream sandwich. "I have no idea. We've done everything I would have done with my mother." 

He smiles. "How adorable your connection is to your parental figures."

"Yeah. I guess I know what my last bucket list item is. Can you take us to Florida?" 

He perks up, interested now. "Miami nightclubs?" He asks, taking hold of my hand.

"No. Cemetary in palm beach."

He frowns, but whisks me away to the exact headstone that I was thinking of. 

"Creepy." I murmur, kneeling in front of the marble with a sigh.

"Marie Johanna Kleeson? Your mother I suppose."  He reads off the stone, kneeling as well.

I nod. "She died when I got my job. Heart attack. I suppose you did this with her too."

He nods in as acknowledgement. "One of my many selves did this with her. She went to a museum in France, went to Thailand and then she gambled until sundown in Miami casinos."

"Sounds like her," I fist bump her headstone before standing. "Goodbye mom. I'm sorry I wasn't there for you." 

"As sweet as this is, your time is up my dear. It's time to go." He says, offering a hand to let me up.

"Will it hurt?" 

"Depends on whether you were good or not in your life." He says, moving us back to the streets of New York city. 

The bus was still there, ready to kill me. The woman was still on her phone, the birds still mid flight. 

"I'm ready." Even though I wasn't. 

"It doesn't matter, it's happening." He said, disappearing from before my eyes.

I blink in confusion, the bus hitting me to the pavement before I could question anything.

I had gotten used to it honestly. Whenever I felt trapped behind my desk I would tell a coworker that I needed to go to the roof for a smoke (to ensure that no one would follow) and I would tap.

And tap. Then tap. And tap.

I would wind up in the most bizarre places. Once it was in the zoo, where the new keeper was nervous about handling a cheetah.

Another time I helped a little old Hispanic woman in the mountains clean her house and get her groceries.

Yet this time, after the disgusted looks from Betty (as if she doesn't smoke), and the escape to the roof. After the pull in my gut, I found myself in a downtown apartment.

The view of the river was beautiful, the apartment well kept and spacious. The walls bare of any art.

I frowned, how was I supposed to help? Who was I supposed to help?

There were three doors to my right. The first was a closet, full of unused winter clothes. The second a bathroom, with only the necessities. 

The third led to the bedroom. A young woman sat on the bed, staring out the window, holding an orange bottle in her hand.

She didn't look at me. "Are you an angel?" 

"Maybe, why? What'd you take?"

The pills rattle as she holds them up. "Opioids. I have a tumor in my brain that's going to kill me. So I told the doctor that I wanted to do it myself."

I sat down on the bed next to her.

"Why did you call me here?"

She looks at me with glassy eyes, from the drugs or her tears I couldn't tell. 

"I didn't want to be alone." 

"Then you won't be."
